lesson.intuition: A homogeneous Poisson process counts arrivals with independent stationary increments and rate lambda. Its count over length t has Poisson mean and variance lambda t; its interarrival times are independent exponential variables of mean 1/lambda. A renewal process allows other independent identically distributed positive interarrival laws. Then memorylessness usually disappears. For finite positive mean interarrival time mu, the renewal rate approaches 1/mu under standard renewal assumptions; that is a long-run statement, not an exact finite-time count formula.

lesson.intuition: A martingale is an integrable process adapted to an information filtration whose conditional expected next value equals its present value. It models fairness relative to available information, not a path that stays constant. A submartingale has conditional next expectation at least the present value. Standard Brownian motion starts at zero, has continuous paths and independent Gaussian increments with mean zero and variance equal to elapsed time. Brownian paths are almost surely nowhere differentiable, so ordinary velocity is not defined. Optional stopping needs conditions; choosing a stopping rule does not automatically preserve expectation.

lesson.intuition: A linear operator between normed spaces is bounded when one constant C controls ||Tx||≤C||x|| for every input. This is equivalent to continuity. Its operator norm is the supremum over the unit ball. The continuous dual consists of bounded linear scalar-valued functionals. On a Hilbert space the Riesz representation theorem identifies each continuous functional with an inner-product vector, with a convention-dependent conjugation in complex spaces. In infinite dimensions linearity alone does not imply boundedness, and dense definitions must be distinguished from operators defined on the whole space.

lesson.intuition: For a bounded operator T on a complex Banach space, its spectrum consists of scalars lambda for which T-lambda I has no bounded inverse on the whole space. In finite dimensions these are eigenvalues; in infinite dimensions spectral points may have no eigenvector. Compact self-adjoint operators on a Hilbert space admit orthonormal eigenvector structure, with any nonzero eigenvalues real, of finite multiplicity and accumulating only at zero. The kernel must be included. These hypotheses matter: a general bounded operator need not have an eigenbasis.
